item.title: The case for export controls has retreated all the way down to a single premise that still holds
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cogrev-出口管制的理由一路退守-只剩一个前提说得通/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cogrev-出口管制的理由一路退守-只剩一个前提说得通/
item.description: First it was about preventing military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.
item.content:encoded:
First it was about preventing military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.

A three-hour debrief on a China trip; the back half on the mechanics of US-China policy — the drift in the rationale for controls, decoupling risk, and alternatives — is more worth hearing than the travelogue up front.

8:56 What the China discourse lacks is a target state
Nathan says the missing piece in America's discussion of China is a ‘target state’: everyone jumps straight to ‘we want to win’, but nobody answers what winning looks like, what happens if we lose, or whether there is an achievable condition for victory. His proposed goal is Pax Machina, or better, Pax Robotica — the two countries and the world sharing the prosperity and peace of the AI era, robots into factories, into fields, into homes, while avoiding the AI version of the sword of Damocles. He is explicit that this is not about winning, it is about arriving together. A competition with no target state leaves only escalation itself.

18:56 China is not rising, it is returning to historical normal
To the claim that ‘China can't innovate’, Nathan applies one word: cope, and says it is isomorphic to cope in the AI debate — conceding that AI has come this far while insisting it won't reason, won't discover new knowledge, won't change paradigms. His judgment is that China's return is the long-run historical norm, and that the period he and Dario grew up in — China down, America the sole superpower — was the anomaly. Any effort to slow China's progress can therefore work at most in the short term; China will be a first-tier player in nearly every major human domain. This is not a prediction, it is, in his view, something already locked in by historical structure.

28:44 On purchasing power, China is half again as large as the US
In dollar-denominated GDP, the US is about 30 trillion and China about 20 trillion, so the US is 50% larger; on purchasing power parity, China is about 45 trillion against the US's 30 trillion, so China is 50% larger. Nathan says a good meal for two in Shanghai can come in under $10, which is impossible in New York, San Francisco, or even Detroit, so the PPP measure is closer to reality. A more concrete picture: a roughly 45-minute pedicure costs about $12, and the young employee in her twenties at the shop pulls out an iPhone 17 — the iPhone 17 is not cheaper in China than in the US, and high-end Xiaomi and Huawei phones also approach a thousand dollars. His explanation is the one-child structure, with the wealth of four grandparents plus two parents concentrated on one person.

1:25:10 The chip ban hits a century of humiliation
China sees itself as a top-tier civilisation that spent most of history at the technological frontier; it missed once and was invaded, forced to accept opium, with the European powers and Japan as the perpetrators — and someone who was 20 when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976 is still alive today. The core lesson is that you cannot fall behind at the technological frontier: ‘we are never going back’. Huawei is the tech champion under this framework: the first to genuinely reach the top of a global frontier industry, only to be blocked by the US pressuring allies over espionage risk, when Snowden has already proven that the US listens to everyone. The chip ban is the same script again: AI is barely off the ground, there isn't even an agent that can reliably book a flight, and the ban comes first. Nathan says this is not Xi Jinping's view alone; it has seeped into educated society. He also concedes that American companies' grievance over stolen IP is entirely legitimate.

1:35:23 China doesn't talk about an AI race, it talks about public goods
Nathan did not hear a single person the whole trip say China is ahead, or that China will win; almost nobody even framed AI as a race. What he heard was prosperity, material abundance, how to care for an aging population. In a mall he asked a car company's staff about autonomous driving, and they volunteered that ‘but Tesla is better’. At WAIC, Xi's speech opened by noting that the field of AI began at Dartmouth College in the US — he could have left it out, and careful observers read it as an olive branch; another line was that countries should jointly oppose ‘over-extending the concept of national security in the AI domain’. China's hardest signal so far is open weights: take them, run them for free, fine-tune them however you like, and once they're out you can't take them back. Nathan says this is both a sincere wish and a strategic position, quite credible now, but entirely capable of changing later.

2:11:27 The rationale for export controls keeps retreating
Nathan thinks export controls do have an effect, but mainly in the future — the large-scale expansion of chip capacity hasn't landed yet. What he really objects to is the drift in the policy's rationale: initially preventing military applications, then retreating to stopping frontier models, now retreating to limiting how many AI agents China can run; that sounds like an attempt to suppress the Chinese public, to keep Chinese companies and individuals from using the tools Americans use themselves. The only self-consistent premise for this policy is a belief that we are in a short race toward godlike superintelligence and that whoever gets there first takes all — which is basically Anthropic's belief, so Dario advocating these policies is not self-contradictory: he genuinely believes recursive self-improvement kicks off in '27 or '28. Nathan concedes he can follow the logic, but still argues for slowing the frontier together instead.

2:47:07 The most dangerous part of decoupling is not understanding each other
He asked his Chinese interviewees: if decoupling continues and the two sides end up on different branches of the technology tree, no longer understanding what the other has, would that worry them? The answer was ‘not yet’; when would it? ‘When China's chip ecosystem is good enough that we can do our own thing entirely.’ From this he derives the core risk: a hardware fork drags along a hardware-algorithm co-design fork, and add to that China stopping open weights and stopping publishing in English, and it may not take long to reach a point where ‘we don't know the shape, architecture or capabilities of each other's AI’. At that point both sides would genuinely be right to panic, and genuinely right to race.

3:07:25 Replace the arms race with a disease medal table
He starts with a rule: don't train LLMs to maximise money-making on the open internet, and don't train AI to accomplish military objective x by any means necessary — that is training the very thing we fear most to seize power. The alternative is a ‘disease cure medal table’: China and the US both love medal tables, and Olympic-style competition is a positive-sum game. The table could be most cancer types cured, most diseases cured, highest energy-density battery, lowest annual traffic deaths. He says this needs very little capital to catalyse and could be offered unilaterally as a global public good. The landing point: he doesn't care whether the cancer cure comes from China or the US, he just wants cancer cured.

item.title: You Can't Build Superintelligence Inside a Data Centre: The Bottleneck Is Real-World Signal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.description: Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.

Tom Reed pushes the argument that ‘signal is sovereign’ all the way to the end, and it will change how you judge AGI timelines and AI lab strategy; the analogies are sharp and the density is high.

2:54 The bottleneck for the singularity is signal, not compute
Tom's positive claim is not that superintelligence is impossible, but that it cannot be stacked up inside a data centre. His mechanism: to be good at solving problems, you need a source of problems, and that source can only be hard interaction with the real world in serial time. He compresses this into one line — ‘signal is sovereign’ — bodies need pain, companies need profit, models need real deployment. So he judges that the arrival of superintelligence depends on deploying AI into the economy expensively, painfully and slowly, not on how much more compute gets piled up inside a lab.

5:01 Jaggedness will not disappear before the singularity
The current way capabilities advance does not support the claim that ‘the model is accumulating a general g’: models only get better at the things they have a chance to practise, so the capability boundary is more uneven than anyone expected. In 2016 nobody would have predicted a model that beats Stanford Law graduates on the bar exam yet cannot play tic-tac-toe reliably. Tom thinks jaggedness is mainly a product of the training data distribution, and there is no reason to believe automating AI R&D would end it, so he proposes Toner's Law: we should expect jaggedness to persist longer than expected, even once we have adjusted for it.

6:01 Patchwork RL will not buy you general intelligence
Tom zeroes in on the current toolbox for capability progress: custom RL environments are the main engine. In Mechanize's telling, each environment is a single engineer spending a week patching one specific failure observed on a real frontier model; in Zhengdong Wang's telling, scaling used to hand you a bundle of capabilities, and now you unlock them one at a time with effort. Tom's challenge: are we really going to do the singularity one problem per week at a time? If RL really generalised, AI companies should have shown evidence by now; when Dwarkesh kept pressing Dario, every one of Dario's rebuttals was just a weak analogy between RL and the pretraining generalisation of the GPT-2 era.

8:26 For most tasks the relevant data is zero
The common rebuttal is that LLMs are wildly sample-inefficient and could improve a lot, and AI bulls point smugly at DeepSeek reaching GPT-4 level on a fraction of the compute. Tom does not buy it: Anson Ho and Beren Millidge both point out that gains in intelligence per FLOP come mainly from data quality rather than algorithm quality, and pure algorithmic innovation yields fairly weak returns at constant compute. More fundamentally, for most tasks the relevant data simply does not exist — improving sample efficiency by orders of magnitude still multiplies zero. His test: if the internet had never existed, how much progress could today's talent and compute make on writing code? His guess is tens of billions of human-hours.

11:40 Text about a task is not the task
For most economically interesting tasks, what is in the corpus is description, commentary or advice, not a record of performing the task itself. Dominion is a board game with a huge amount of strategy writing, yet Claude plays it badly: the training process that teaches it to write beautiful articles about Dominion is a different thing from building an agent that can win, because the optimisation target is ‘the advice looks good’ rather than ‘the strategy wins’. Tom's analogy is that the relationship between LLMs and most tasks is a bit like the relationship between McKinsey and running a company. The exception is writing code — the tokens are themselves a constituent part of the task — which is why training AlphaZero on chess commentary rather than games would be the norm.

14:06 Scores go up, real capability does not
How does self-improvement inside a data centre know it has actually got stronger? Of the submissions on SWE-bench accepted by AI automated graders, close to half are rejected by the real human maintainers of the relevant codebase — you can pump the score up while the merge rate does not move. Tom asks in return: how is Claude 8 supposed to tell, from the results of a Become-POTUS eval alone, whether its brilliant new algorithm really improved Claude 9's ability to become president? Evals are useful, but they are always stubbornly incomplete proxies; in the end the only eval that counts is voters, customers, the economy and the P&L. Without those, your singularity gets ruthlessly Goodharted.

15:28 Market data is not hidden, it does not exist yet
The second layer of doubt is more fundamental and more speculative: even an arbitrarily intelligent simulator cannot generate practice data for many tasks, because that data can only be produced through interaction with the relevant market. This is Hayekian: that something is good is a signal generated by millions of actors revealing preferences through behaviour, and it cannot be simulated inside a data centre — it is not that data collection happens to fail, it is that the data does not yet exist anywhere. He uses his own board gaming as the analogy: a game of Twilight Imperium takes 12 hours, he will plan weeks ahead until he feels certain of winning, and about 5 minutes into the real game his predictive power goes to zero. Continual learning does not save you either, because without a genuinely diverse problem set you cannot tell which algorithm is better.

21:17 The winner may be the deployer itself
Corollary one: a policy focus on ‘internal deployment’ and ‘automating AI R&D’ may be misplaced — superintelligence is not impossible, it just will not arrive in the shape currently imagined or on the timeline currently predicted; the next phase looks more like the grind of deployment, customer discovery and real data collection. Corollary two: data holders have far more power than they realise (Ukraine is one example), and the asymmetry between ‘companies that can build frontier models’ and ‘entities holding proprietary deployment data from real economic activity’ may flip. Corollary three: labs may conquer vertical industries one by one, and the way to win is to become the deployer yourself.

item.title: An Account for Every AI Agent: Card Fees Can't Carry the Machine Economy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.description: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and 30 cents is exactly the card minimum — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
item.content:encoded:
Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and 30 cents is exactly the card minimum — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.

The part about how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy. Agent payments come with hard numbers; the new-drug section is more opinion than detail.

6:47 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
Armstrong says agents are already generating lots of few-cent transactions: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialised agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the per-transaction minimum fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. His number: roughly 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest reason stablecoins and crypto rails get to cut into the machine economy.

11:42 Build a "brain" for every service
Coinbase built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test ever run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future cases, and the one-shot PR rate keeps climbing; Armstrong calls this "recursive self-improvement".

15:00 The CEO runs 10 agents on code at once
Armstrong says that when he hits an idea or a bug now, he no longer pings the team all day; he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends over a finished PR for review — he says it's addictive. He has also made the CEO go back to writing features: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten things each, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of doing this podcast, all 10 items got done and were waiting for his review.

17:02 What gets killed is tasks, not people
On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity really is rising, but that's a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He doesn't think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people already there can do vastly more and everything speeds up. At the same time, two-person and five-person companies will indeed produce volumes that used to be unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people can produce far more, and over the long run margins should rise. He doesn't close the door on it — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

18:33 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings reports: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, considers it digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenised-equity product he just announced is currently available only outside the US, and they are talking to regulators about a US path; he stresses these are real equities — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

21:57 Prediction markets are more than sports betting
Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached roughly $100 million in annualised revenue, growing more than 100% quarter over quarter. Sports is indeed part of it, and he thinks that's a form of entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it's much bigger than that, and the societal implications aren't fully understood yet. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation". Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God" — he calls that an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock: you're just betting it will get better or worse.

31:53 Restore cells to their youthful function
New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it doesn't change the cell type (the Yamanaka-lab-style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast space of transcription-factor combinations for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then functional experiments (mostly animal models), and finally human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and immune-system T cells. The first Phase 1 trial is in alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates this one drug alone could be worth $20 billion if it succeeds, but the goal is a 40-year-old with the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

41:10 What America lacks isn't land, it's sandboxes
Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places, over-regulation. He mentions Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and thinks they've had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centres, nuclear plants, unlimited drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item. First try what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to try in, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.

item.title: Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes, not yet in humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.description: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents met — change only the RNA in the brain and you change behavior three generations later.
item.content:encoded:
Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents met — change only the RNA in the brain and you change behavior three generations later.

35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with the experimental designs and key numbers given; on the mammalian part the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a conclusion you can apply.

4:37 The genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out one page
Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's analogy is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out one page, and that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of the RNA that gets transcribed does other things, many of which are still not understood. This distinction is the foundation for everything discussed later — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and the remaining question is whether life experience can rewrite those instructions.

11:35 Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
Why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for the erasure is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being limited to the few pieces one room happened to make.

12:46 It was opposed and also wanted, and not for reasons of data alone
This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is theory, the barrier is sitting right there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He gives Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he doesn't push this into ‘because people want to believe it, it has promise’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

16:20 Nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
Why should you trust nematodes? The conditions Rechavi lists are concrete: a C. elegans is always 959 cells, of which 302 are neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, kept in a dish eating bacteria, with a highly controlled environment, so nature and nurture can be separated; the generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run through hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

21:20 Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses
The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, and if it is destroyed it stays black. First let nematodes be infected by the virus and destroy it, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in the offspring — these offspring have no ability to make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they are still black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happens: all the offspring are black, and the resistance can be passed on for several more generations. Sequencing can directly read those small RNAs matching the viral genome, and only the offspring of parents that had been infected have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

24:46 The brain and inheritance don't speak the same language
The boldest question in this episode is: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something might just mean removing a certain odorant receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been proven convincingly enough, because no one has explained how information gets from the brain to the germ cells. His own route bypasses translation: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of native small RNAs in the nematode brain changed the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them all the way to three generations later, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

28:17 Mammals lack an RNA amplifier
Why can nematodes do it while mammals must be doubted? The mechanism Rechavi gives is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: at that point there are only a few cells, and it might even act on the placenta formed during pregnancy, after which development is steered off course step by step, and problems like metabolism follow. This is the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ line of thinking. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, and time will tell’.

31:07 RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
The applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples preparing to have children do DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but right now no one looks at RNA; if the mechanism were clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, and there might be certain RNAs associated with disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. Only a step further out is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if the mice are made to exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; when doing IVF, perhaps you could change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it were figured out, he has also imagined telling someone preparing for IVF, ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, and that would change your RNA profile.

item.title: Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail, and Retail Theft Has Been Industrialized
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal in stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal in stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation, with plenty of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious, which Scott describes as the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years is that of malicious shrink, roughly 40% comes from internal employees, 35% from people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only within a few points each year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that they have been underreported ever since COVID, with neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capturing it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal, and these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to trade for money — so they will get physical, and they have gotten physical. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and even killed. That's why asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene, just to back off. His attitude is that he would trade shrink for people's safety every single day, and management and the board would back that decision.

23:53 RFID fails the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and still, in 2026, is expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, essentially a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read and only actively transmitting solutions work. He also says tag cost is now almost zero, and the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits costs a fortune. They have tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but to do that for a single power drill you have to rework the entire production line, and it's very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs to go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — which might be a garage, a warehouse, or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a $799 combo kit that has to be restocked 4.2 times for every one sold. Take that to finance and they immediately understand it's a gross margin problem — as long as locking up breaks even or even makes a little money, it's justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon an associate who unlocks it in an average of 90 seconds; and locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the goods are finally there.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can just drive the goods away
On the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where a whole container is rerouted at the port or a transshipment warehouse and taken elsewhere, even loaded back onto a container ship and hauled off; second, a driver goes eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and hauls boxes out; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, made to look real with AI, where a driver pulls in, says he's picking up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new isn't necessarily the methods, it's the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years, with trains sitting in a yard getting broken into by a crowd; and the other side has good intelligence, they don't touch every car, only the ones carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 AI in security is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviors and then recognize the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago no one cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he's very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it's bipartisan, it has passed the House, it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he'll sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources, and the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: no one took it seriously, and the prevailing mood was still decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they cannot do without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they cannot do without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-hundred-year winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable judgment framework, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark and the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some battle; it won through a five-step playbook. First, an open society on an island — the seventeenth-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in. Then global trade: Dutch merchant ships went everywhere, and the wealth was so great that even the paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada across the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot do without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly collapsed.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having its cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own vulnerable point. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast — oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other, pushing hard on solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to keep themselves alive.

25:50 Every round of technological bounty needs a new institution to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is good it raises my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era was matched by the Homestead Act, with the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; what replaced the family farm in the twentieth century was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new machine for distributing wealth. Now that machine has hit housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley is going over to the tech Hamiltonians
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state to clear the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolated in peacetime and fight to the death when hit. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the game. Mead says the new species really worth watching is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees to be patriotic — selling code to China is shameful, and your colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from the old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with more equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time he went to a drone factory and saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; a few months later he went again, and the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers move together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need to build a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people, with a squad of drones alongside hunting the enemy's drones coming to attack. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. Things flip every six months. The bitterest irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is penned in at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On ‘will the mainland attack Taiwan’, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it is willing to cross the threshold — once it fails, it is catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade, doing things that change facts enough without triggering an armed American response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japan's independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor Japan in, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might go soft when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — and deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of national annihilation no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is ‘very interesting and a little confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will overhaul it. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 What actually happens if you or I get ECT
If you or I were to receive ECT, here is the sequence: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in a hospital or outpatient setting, an IV line is placed along with two blood pressure cuffs (arm and right leg), and EKG, EEG and EMG leads are connected. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant such as succinylcholine is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, or even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 Electrode placement, and why the right side comes first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it has fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During a course of treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are too much, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral isn't working well enough, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then probe upward from a low dose until a seizure occurs. But treatment isn't just about reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. The dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted by trial. If in one session a patient's seizure doesn't occur or doesn't last long enough (under 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer.

20:22 We still don't know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still don't fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter changes: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all change markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. Two, large fluctuations in hormones such as ACTH, prolactin and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. The mechanisms may also differ by condition (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), so for now the only option is to keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key numbers are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms fully gone) of 50%-60% and response rates (marked improvement) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the best remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can cut the 30-day readmission rate in half. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression combined with severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Memory problems draw the most attention among side effects
ECT's thorniest side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive function actually improves in the long term — possibly because the depression improves. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) usually recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, which is why many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it typically affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more prone to this problem than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a deadly syndrome that gets misidentified
Catatonia is often simply lumped in as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological illness can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely immobile and mute; they may show posturing or waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there). Because they cannot eat or drink and remain immobile for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from many causes. The girl mentioned earlier with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (the 'Brain on Fire' case) developed catatonia; immunotherapy and lorazepam both failed, and she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT currently faces is finding a place that offers it. His hospital performs more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 sessions per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and adults and children traveling across state lines for care are not few — especially in infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. So improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often don't recognize catatonia and don't dare or don't think to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is part of his daily work.

item.title: The Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that schools are not totalitarian enclaves while also holding that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that schools are not totalitarian enclaves while also holding that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.

Each case gets five or six minutes covering the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment and searches in American public schools in one sitting.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse first
Can students really invoke the First Amendment in class? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge or salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II pushed more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge of allegiance daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and their parents could be fined or even jailed. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6 to 3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe, nor make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students possess some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer text is held unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added Under God to the pledge of allegiance in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short interfaith prayer, and each district decided whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer allowed students to opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale held it unconstitutional 6 to 1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted establishing religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling provoked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest American involvement in the Vietnam War. School officials announced in advance that refusal to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7 to 2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress and grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or demonstrable substantial interference with teaching, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said public schools may not become totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This substantial disruption standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host said on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds rather absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story on teen pregnancy that used pseudonyms but might still make the interviewees identifiable, and a divorce story that named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both full pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that there was no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5 to 3. The key distinction was tolerating student speech versus promoting student speech: this newspaper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed ethically immature as journalism. The Court held that schools may exercise control over what they promote. The rights established in Tinker were thus given their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many of her childhood teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks, and on looking into it found that corporal punishment has still not disappeared in the United States. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's paddle was under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, with one to five swats in principle; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that individual case was excessive, but held that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning was that the Eighth Amendment protects the convicted, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by the harsh facts of criminal conviction and imprisonment; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, and boys, Black students and students with disabilities are struck at significantly higher rates.

33:52 A bag search needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 a 14-year-old student known as TLO in New Jersey was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers and kept looking, found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing, and TLO was ultimately convicted and sentenced to a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6 to 3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause required of police, only the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly where they would be; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Make Criticism Land, Lead With High Standards and Trust

item.description: Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. item.content:encoded:
Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the top.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism himself and grounds the intervention in a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of high information density, with none of the vague communication chicken soup.

1:04 Identity bias makes people underperform on the spot
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and that situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. This worry comes from the situation itself: it depresses performance in tests, sports or intellectual tasks on the spot, and it makes people chronically avoid such situations over time, which in turn shapes who they befriend, where they live, and which schools they send their kids to. The anxiety doesn't come from ability — it comes from the expectation of being defined by the label.

3:10 Social media lets labels chase you from every direction
Social media's power lies in how fast it spreads sketches of what a group is like. People have no patience to see the full picture and the exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the number of situations where you might be seen through your identity. Occasionally it also spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone skews negative. The result is that in a diverse society, everyone is more on guard about their own identity and about what others might be thinking.

6:16 A 15-minute self-affirmation exercise raises grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students live with the constant possibility that their ability is being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend just 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they valued most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the opportunity to let the teacher know "I'm not just that label," and their grades began to rise — which fed a positive loop: better grades → less vigilance about the label → still better grades. The intervention cost almost nothing, yet it changed long-term trajectories.

9:20 Vigilance in diverse settings: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. In settings where people of different backgrounds are together and the outcome matters, people oscillate between two choices: remember that "others might read me through my group's stereotype" to protect themselves, or simply forget it, relax, and trust the person in front of them. This isn't fragility — it's real pressure coming from the situation. When the setting matters, it continuously drains attention that should be going to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback work
In the experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. The first two ways of giving it — straight criticism, or criticism preceded by a "positive buffer" — were trusted by white students but deeply distrusted by Black students. The third way added just one line: "We have high standards, because the essays will be published; I read your essay and I believe you can reach them." Under that condition, Black students took their essays home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 You can't assume others already trust you
After years as a dean and provost, Claude considers the most useful skill to be realizing that everyone you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, when in reality people worry about how you view the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are good at giving that signal first: even if an employee disagrees with a decision, as long as they feel the other person respects who they are and their potential, the team atmosphere is completely different.

17:35 Let people see you as a person before you talk trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what this situation means to them — when power is unequal, the person with more power must send the safety signal first; second, near-obsessive clarity, because beating around the bush destroys valuable information; third, warmth and goodwill, because people need to confirm the other side is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connection, clarity, care.
