item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-eyeonai-乌克兰最大无人机商-月产近10万架-ai拦截是第一步/
item.description: Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, and its interceptors take down Russian Shaheds costing over $50,000 at a cost of about $2,000 each. AI guidance is already in combat, but full autonomy is still far off.
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, and its interceptors take down Russian Shaheds costing over $50,000 at a cost of about $2,000 each. AI guidance is already in combat, but full autonomy is still far off.

This episode is a rare first-hand account from a leading Ukrainian drone manufacturer about what battlefield drones actually look like, what they cost, and where the boundaries of AI use lie. It is information-dense and directly useful for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.

4:07 Nearly 100,000 a month, and capacity is still expanding
General Cherry was founded in 2023 and initially produced only about 10 drones a month; today monthly output reaches roughly 100,000 (the exact figure is confidential). The company has worked with more than 110 military brigades, and the best units consume more than 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still rising, because battlefield consumption is enormous and drones have become expendables.

7:09 Ukraine has hundreds of drone companies, but only 10-15 at the top
The number of drone companies in Ukraine may be as high as 2,000, but the vast majority are garage-scale workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can actually produce 1,000 to 10,000 units a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented yet enormous industrial ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means fierce competition.

8:14 AI models are built in-house, co-created deeply with the military
General Cherry's AI guidance system is entirely self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and built in close cooperation with different military units at the front. Mobile teams gather battlefield feedback every day so products can be iterated quickly. This ‘R&D-combat-feedback’ loop lets Ukrainian drone technology adapt rapidly to battlefield changes rather than relying on external procurement.

10:20 The rocket-shaped FPV came from Red Bull, not Ukraine
This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian invention; Red Bull first used it in sports events in 2021 or 2022. Ukrainian companies found that the shape could reach higher speeds than ordinary quadcopters, so they adopted and optimised it. This reflects the rapid learning and pragmatism of Ukraine's drone industry — it does not chase originality, only effectiveness.

17:24 A $2,000 interceptor against a $50,000 Shahed
General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as Bullet) cost about $2,000 but can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is Ukraine's key strategy for countering Russian ‘saturation attacks’ — using cheap drones to consume the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding the waste of expensive Western air-defence missiles.

21:28 Interceptors have confirmed more than 5,000 Russian shootdowns
Since entering production in February 2025, General Cherry's tactical interceptor drone (General Trajectory Air) has confirmed more than 5,000 Russian drone shootdowns, including more than 1,000 Russian ‘Moniya’ drones in December alone. The Shahed-intercepting model also entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed shootdowns approaching 1,000. These numbers show that interceptor drones have become an important force in battlefield air defence.

23:28 The AI runs on the device, not in the cloud
General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's local camera chip, not in the cloud. After an operator detects a target by radar and launches the drone, the AI automatically identifies and locks onto the target without human intervention. This on-device AI design avoids battlefield communication latency and jamming, and is the key to making it viable in real combat.

27:32 Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is now unavoidable
Marko admits that if drones became fully autonomous it would be terrifying — killing would no longer require another person, only a robot or a drone. At present they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs significantly raises cost, and it is better to buy a few more without AI. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will fall, making future battlefields even more brutal.

item.title: The Wow! Signal Hasn't Been Settled in Nearly 50 Years: It Looks Like an Alien Call, but No Second One Ever Came
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-isaacarthur-wow信号近50年没落定-它像外星呼叫-却再没来第二声/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-isaacarthur-wow信号近50年没落定-它像外星呼叫-却再没来第二声/
item.description: That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the threshold for evidence of an alien civilization; its legacy isn't an answer but a reminder that in a noisy universe, the distance between detection and proof is an entire galaxy.
item.content:encoded:
That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the threshold for evidence of an alien civilization; its legacy isn't an answer but a reminder that in a noisy universe, the distance between detection and proof is an entire galaxy.

Anyone hoping for a verdict will be disappointed; anyone wanting to understand how a single anomaly does or doesn't become evidence gets a complete framework for judgment here.

3:09 The 72-second length comes from Earth's rotation
Big Ear was a transit telescope: it didn't turn to track a target, it let Earth's rotation sweep the whole sky past overhead. A point source fixed on the celestial sphere crossing the beam naturally takes about 72 seconds — exactly 1/1200 of a day. So the duration doesn't mean the sender deliberately spoke for only 72 seconds; what really matters is the gain curve: a real source enters the beam, strengthens, leaves the beam, weakens. The Wow! signal matched that whole profile, and any later terrestrial-interference explanation has to clear that bar first.

5:10 6EQUJ5 is an intensity curve, not a cipher
6EQUJ5 is the signal-strength reading under Big Ear's early print format: each symbol represents roughly a 12-second observation window, and the digits and letters indicate the multiple above background noise. In time order they are 6, 14, 26, 30, 19, 5 — strong in the middle, weak at both ends, like a brightness curve written sideways. Renormalized to 1–100, that's 17, 40, 74, 86, 54, 14. The host's quip is worth remembering: if the aliens' first sentence looks like a failed software activation code, that's a reasonable opening too.

7:11 It hugs the hydrogen line, yet sits 50 kHz off
1420 MHz is the radio spectral line of neutral hydrogen, the natural landmark of the universe's most abundant element, and the frequency SETI most often assumes a call would use. Because Big Ear had its master oscillator set 0.1 MHz high, the Wow! signal's frequency has two corrected values: 1420.356 MHz or 1420.456 MHz; the true hydrogen line sits at about 1420.406 MHz. Either way it's only about 50 kHz off, as if deliberately avoiding hydrogen noise while using the hydrogen line as a coordinate. But that neighborhood is also full of natural hydrogen-cloud signal sources, and frequency alone can't distinguish cleverness from coincidence.

11:13 One horn received it, the other didn't
Big Ear had two feed horns side by side. A source fixed on the celestial sphere, swept past by Earth's rotation, should enter the two horns in sequence and be recorded twice. The Wow! signal appeared in only one horn, and the records don't say which, so the sky retains two candidate positions. Possible reasons include: the source itself lit up only briefly, a narrow beam happened to graze by, or the interference came from nearby. Every later search — including Breakthrough Listen's 2022 hunt for sun-like stars in the candidate region with Green Bank and the Allen array — heard no repeat. The missing second detection is the core reason it can't make the confirmed list.

15:17 Terrestrial interference and satellites are both hard to mimic
Earth is noisy, but a genuine candidate has to pass the 72-second profile test: an ordinary aircraft crossing the beam wouldn't take such a convenient time; a low-orbit satellite usually sweeps through in just seconds. For a satellite to do it, it would need to be in high orbit, coming in via a side lobe, or on a special orbit — a whole chain of coincidences. Terrestrial transmissions are banned in the internationally protected 1420 MHz band, but illegal equipment or faulty electronics could produce out-of-band signals that leak in through an antenna side lobe. There's also an effect called interstellar scintillation that can briefly brighten a distant signal, but that requires an amplified source to exist in the first place. None of these explanations is perfect, which is exactly why the puzzle survives.

19:18 A magnetar could pump a hydrogen cloud into a maser
Research drawing on Arecibo archives has produced a natural explanation: some high-energy transient — a magnetar flare, say — pumps atoms in a cold neutral hydrogen cloud into a population inversion, briefly turning the cloud into a natural microwave maser, much as a laser amplifies microwaves. This can explain several things at once: the signal came from space, sat near the hydrogen line, was strong enough, yet appeared only once; the hydrogen cloud was glowing as the first horn swept past and had gone dark by the time the second horn arrived. The host says this is his personal favorite, because it solves multiple problems within one mechanism, but it remains a speculative path with no conclusive evidence.

27:27 Becoming a discovery means passing four gates
If a signal like this arrives again, calling it a true technosignature would require at least four conditions: one, it repeats at the same position, so we know it's still there; two, telescopes at two different locations receive it simultaneously, ruling out Earth interference; three, the signal carries modulation, encoding or mathematical structure, rather than being a bare carrier; four, known natural processes are ruled out one by one. Historically, when pulsars were first discovered they were nicknamed "little green men," showing that nature can perfectly impersonate intelligence. The right posture isn't to pick a side between belief and mockery, but to allow the excitement and then do everything possible to prove you're fooling yourself.

31:29 Its legacy is a window that was far too narrow
The Wow! signal appeared for 72 seconds in exactly the form early SETI hoped to recognize — narrowband, near the hydrogen line, strong enough, shaped like a real source in the sky — and then nothing more. It showed what a great discovery might look like before the evidence is complete. The host's landing point: the galaxy is a hundred thousand light-years wide and billions of years old, and even the largest civilization is just one flickering spark within it. If civilizations don't expand, don't transmit often, and don't often point a beam at us, the Fermi paradox may not exist at all. With that 1/1200 of a day, the Wow! signal briefly put that possibility in front of humanity.

item.title: Land Is Not a Commodity: Why a Land Value Tax Can Cure the Housing Crisis
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.description: The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden off buildings and onto land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.
item.content:encoded:
The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden off buildings and onto land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.

The land value tax is an overlooked lever that economists on both left and right agree on. Lars Doucet uses Houston parking lots, South Korea's appraisal system, and Norway's resource dividend to turn an abstract tax regime into a contest over power.

0:05 A land tax is not a property tax, it is a location tax
Lars builds his case on an analogy: the land value tax and the ordinary property tax share an origin, but the LVT splits ‘building value’ from ‘land value’. A building tax punishes you for constructing, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax only punishes you for occupying a good location and letting it sit idle. He says land value comes from the labor of the people around you — your ability to earn a living, go to school, and make friends the moment you walk out the door depends entirely on your neighbors and the whole city. The landlord lies back and sucks that collective value into his own pocket, and that is the paradox of Progress and Poverty: the ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does.

0:13 The YIMBYs are right, but not right enough
The host asks: Auckland upzoned and rents fell, so do we still need a land tax? Lars concedes the ‘housing shortage’ is the main cause, but points out that YIMBYs never explain one counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet its downtown still holds a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and building together, so the more you build the more tax you pay, while sitting on it and waiting for appreciation is cheaper. So developers have no incentive to develop, only an incentive to lobby for rezoning and then keep hoarding. He says reform without a land tax ends in a stalemate: ‘you changed the zoning, but I just won't sell.’

0:23 The objections are built on imagination
Lars sorts the opposition into three camps and dismantles each. How do you appraise land separately from buildings? He says 14,000 appraisal jurisdictions worldwide already do something like it: South Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels a year and produces nationwide land values in 5 months; Norway trained a national automated valuation model on the state property data platform Finn.no with a core team of just 3 people. Think there will be too many protests? He says the real source of protest is ‘my land looks the same as my neighbor's, why charge me more’ — under a land tax, you and your neighbor are assessed on the same location basis, which actually makes it easier. The excuse for not doing it is that nobody has measured it.

0:35 The little old lady is not an argument against it
The sharpest criticism is ‘the transition is unfair’ — on the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalized value of all future tax liability, which amounts to expropriation in one stroke. Lars concedes this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers the safeguard: the move is never a one-step nationwide 100% land tax, but a gradual switch by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations and most single-family homes actually see their tax bill fall. As for the elderly afraid of being driven out of their old homes, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: you owe it, and it is deducted with interest from your estate when you die.

0:41 Britain's failure was a capacity problem
The most commonly cited counterexample online is Britain's 1910s ‘People's Budget’: the valuation took 6 years and was overturned by shopkeepers' protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: the much-shared article is simply ‘deriving a universal law from a sample of one’, and it simultaneously claims that ‘a pure land tax has never succeeded’ and that ‘land cannot be valued’ — yet South Korea has been appraising nationwide land values parcel by parcel for decades. He says this only proves the British state machine was weak, not that a land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, don't pass off lazy ignorance as a verdict.

0:45 Norway achieves Georgism through a resource dividend
Lars points to a fact that makes Norway a ‘success story’ today: Norway's entire resource management regime is Georgist in structure — oil and other natural resources are deemed the property of all the people, and extractors pay extremely high resource taxes, but production and investment themselves are not punished, so entrepreneurship is encouraged while the natural bounty is captured for the treasury and funds universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except that it is not on land value. This ‘Norwegian paradox’ leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state, it can be its foundation.

0:51 The automobile opened a second frontier
Lars explains why the land question that gripped every city 100 years ago later vanished: the frontier itself is a mechanism of ‘free land’ — as long as you can still expand into the wilderness, the poor don't have to face the squeeze of ‘high wages plus high rent’. America's first frontier was westward expansion, and when it closed Henry George appeared; in the 20th century the automobile turned the suburbs into a ‘second frontier’ that lasted another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006-2008. He says people now call this a ‘second Gilded Age’, but it is just a script from over a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work as a ‘third frontier’ held out for only about 5 minutes before capital digested it.

0:53 Don't win online, do the politicians' homework
The closing answer to the last question is very practical: Lars says the most effective way to create change he has learned in the past 5 years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but taking every objection a state senator or city council member might raise, running the data simulations in advance, preparing the answers, and putting them directly on their desks — he calls ‘doing politicians' homework’ an absurd but extraordinarily effective strategy. Several states have now passed bills allowing land value tax reform. His call to action: go measure, don't guess.

item.description: Most people assume it's wealth ambition that carries founders through. Paul Graham says what actually pushes people forward day to day is disaster fear — the server going down, the model train about to fall off the table; keep your head down for ten years, look up and do the math, and you're already a billionaire at the last round's valuation.
item.content:encoded:
Most people assume it's wealth ambition that carries founders through. Paul Graham says what actually pushes people forward day to day is disaster fear — the server going down, the model train about to fall off the table; keep your head down for ten years, look up and do the math, and you're already a billionaire at the last round's valuation.

After 21 years and 47 batches, PG's judgment: AI has changed almost nothing about startups except the bill. Useful for calibrating your confidence in "this time is different."

2:02 People nostalgic for the golden age forget it had only Reddit
Since roughly 2008 people have been saying YC is finished — PG's read is that its attackers have to first admit it was once good, so all they can ever say is "not what it used to be." But his counterexample is concrete: the flagship of the supposed good old days was Reddit, whereas the projects he did office hours with this episode include intercontinental ballistic freight — like an ICBM, except it doesn't explode on landing, it unloads. Another category is curing cancer. He says there are too many ways to go at it — vaccines at one end, therapies at the other — so you should fund several, and any one that works is worth it. This episode had a company doing on-demand research for cancer patients, and what he liked was exactly that approach: cancer is famously not solved by "coming up with a cure," and maybe the way to beat it is death by a thousand cuts.

4:09 Google won't be breached, it will be made obsolete by the world
Many of the ideas in the 2012 "frighteningly ambitious" list have already been done, and one of them was "the new Google." PG says he predicted the path back then: you can't attack Google head-on, you can only wait for the world to change until its model goes out of date. OpenAI is that change itself — after using it he found he no longer uses search, because what he always wanted wasn't web pages, it was information, so he just asks the AI. This is a corollary that holds for every incumbent: moats aren't breached, they're made obsolete.

6:15 Ambition is the ticket in; the daily fuel is fear of looking like a fool
Ambition is a necessity, because the obstacles in startups are too terrifying and sheer conscientiousness won't carry you. But PG says what actually gets a founder moving at any given moment isn't "if I solve this I'll become a billionaire," it's disaster fear: the server is down, the fear of looking like an idiot. His image is a toy train — the engine is going off the edge of the table and you lunge to catch it. You keep your head down fixing the train for ten years, look up and do the math on the last round's valuation, and discover you're already a billionaire. He says sometimes he's the one who does the math first and tells the founder.

9:21 The only test of formidable is whether they get what they want
Formidable is a private word PG and Jessica used before YC. His definition is operational: this person gets what they want in any situation — if they can't, what does formidable even mean. That definition incidentally explains the investing logic: you hold stock in his company, he holds it too, interests are aligned; he gets what he wants, you get what you want. It's also the precondition for his answer to "where does the next trillion-dollar company come from."

11:24 Lean startup isn't dead: even rocket companies can start small
Asked whether lean startup is dead and whether you now have to burn big money from day one, PG's rebuttal has two layers. One is price: tokens are expensive now only because of the GPU shortage, and the price for the same level of inference will fall by roughly 30x a year, and on top of that you're getting higher-quality tokens — technology always gets cheaper. Two is the path: even rocket companies can start with not much money; you can't build a real rocket, but you can produce a design, run simulations, show it to experts, and if it's convincing enough you get the next round. StarCloud wrote a white paper and booked a launch — though he adds that that founder is himself a well-known expert in the field with built-in credibility, and a fresh graduate doesn't have it that easy.

13:24 AI went the wrong direction: from human toward perfect
People doing AI in the 1980s thought the path started from "the perfect fly": able to do only what a fly does, but as well as a fly does it; then climb up to mouse, cat, monkey, human, each level perfect. What we got was the reverse — a complete human right out of the gate, just talking nonsense, like an undergrad trying to bluff his way through a paper. What got optimized was the opposite dimension: not from perfect toward human, but from human toward perfect. That also explains the jagged frontier: it can solve hard math problems but can't tell you what time a restaurant opens.

16:30 AI changes the bill structure, not the shipping speed
PG says the best predictor of startup success is still shipping speed, and AI hasn't replaced that metric — with these tools in hand, plenty of companies this episode still aren't shipping fast enough, which shows the difference isn't how fast you can write things, you first have to come up with the ideas. "With AI, what's still unchanged?" His answer: so far almost everything is exactly the same. The only strange new thing is the bill structure — the biggest cost of a startup used to be salaries, everything else was cheap by comparison; now there's GPUs on top, and tokens can burn tens of thousands of dollars a day.

19:36 The next trillion-dollar company comes from the right person, not the right idea
Asked where the next trillion-dollar company will come from, PG swaps the question from sector to person: it comes from the right founder, not some particular idea — startup ideas are highly variable, and all he'll say is "probably not dog-walking." Conversely, to judge whether a company is worth investing in, first judge whether the founder is formidable, and what they're doing is probably promising. As for whether future founders will look different, he says there's already 20 years of data, today's founders are exactly the same as 20 years ago, and there's no reason the next 20 years will be different.

item.title: Arm Moves Into Making CPUs: The Biggest Bottleneck in Chip Design Is Verification, Not Design
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.description: The real time sink in a chip cycle is verification, debug and documentation, not RTL; 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily, and Arm is breaking its 98.5%-gross-margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.
item.content:encoded:
The real time sink in a chip cycle is verification, debug and documentation, not RTL; 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily, and Arm is breaking its 98.5%-gross-margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.

It uses real internal Arm data to explain what AI is actually good for in chip design, then ties product, capital and supply-chain judgments into one closed loop — worth checking against your own expectations if you work in AI infrastructure.

3:43 Arm is building CPUs itself because customers are pushing it to
Arm used to only sell IP licenses, at 98.5% gross margin, never touching inventory or wafers. One step forward, its compute subsystem already had customers grabbing pre-assembled CPU, GPU and memory "subsystems" as modules; another step forward, because "customers who want a general-purpose CPU for the large-model era can't find a supplier" and came straight to Arm to push for one. Before announcing, it asked almost every license customer, and opposition was minimal: a bigger software ecosystem benefits every customer, so Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft and Google — all companies making Arm server chips — publicly supported it.

8:07 Banning AI tools is sending engineers back to the library
A full chip design cycle is 24-36 months; the most time-consuming parts are not RTL generation or architecture mapping but verification, validation, debug and documentation. AI is especially suited to these steps, and roughly 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily; turning the tools off is like telling people in the 1990s they can only use the internet two hours a day and must spend the rest downstairs in the library. AI is currently weakest at RTL generation and physical design, because models depend on public corpora while the industry's most critical details are private data — exactly the gap companies like Arm can fill.

10:35 From idea to layout is a five-year wait, not two or three
The host asked: once AI eats verification, the most time-consuming step, can 24-36 months shrink to 6-12 months? Rene Haas gave a measured answer: 2-3 years is unrealistic; five years or more, for designs with not-too-complex constraints, going from idea all the way to GDSII (the layout file handed to the fab) is possible. If you type into the tool "make a chip 10% faster, 20% cheaper and 30% more power-efficient than some reference," don't expect one-click completion. His judgment is that in 5-10 years the whole industry's design methodology will visibly change.

15:00 AI supply and demand are still far apart; the bottleneck is the construction site, not the wafer
Discussing the AI bubble, Rene Haas argued for separating valuation froth at the stock level from the industry chain itself; he said explicitly that supply versus demand is still "far apart." Transformer inference and training consume both compute and memory, and demand won't stop. The real hard constraint will move to data-center construction: many projects are being delayed and need more workers, and resistance limiting new data-center builds is appearing in various places; over the next 3-5 years the constraint may not be wafer capacity or memory but the physical build-out staying tight.

17:14 SoftBank doing cloud is becoming a customer for chip companies
For asset-heavy, capex-intensive chip/AI founders: capital availability is itself a gate, and strategic partnerships need to reach early into three layers — supply chain, PE and banks. Behind Arm is SoftBank, and not just as a shareholder; SoftBank has just announced it will build a "neo cloud"-style cloud service, which lets young chip companies avoid only knocking on Microsoft/Google's door for a design win and instead form a direct customer relationship with the Arm/SoftBank ecosystem — one more path to landing.

21:25 Humanoids won't unify; specialized robots will coexist long-term
Rene Haas sees robot 1.0 as purpose-built: mechanics and software both optimized for a single action, and changing a production line means almost starting over. A new generation of robots that can redefine tasks through training, with mechanical bodies that are also general-purpose, will first eat repetitive labor in construction, infrastructure and security. Form factor won't go in a single direction: factories, warehouses and tools are all designed to human dimensions, so humanoids have an advantage; another set of tasks is better served by specialized forms. Cost must come down first, and delivery and warehousing will be the earliest automated scenarios.

27:13 Restricting chips to China is an unwinnable infinite game
On US manufacturing he is direct: the US should build more fabs at home, needed for both national security and supply-chain diversification. On export controls, he talks about an "infinite game" — restricting chips to China cannot produce a victory with an end state, and may instead push key technology out of the US. He also rejects the idea that data centers are "big warehouses with no jobs": energy, liquid cooling and the surrounding ecosystem are all jobs that can be created in the US.

36:00 In a token world, every path goes through a CPU
If you use the token factory metaphor for accelerators, Rene Haas thinks the real system question is: who orchestrates and arbitrates where those tokens go, and delivers them to users. He believes every path goes through a CPU: beyond training, there is inference scheduling, system orchestration, context and tool calls. At the edge, on devices that can't fit a 50W GPU, Arm's power advantage is even clearer. The CPU hasn't disappeared; it's forming persistent demand alongside accelerators.

item.title: The Number One Fraud Red Flag Isn't Greed — It's Personal Finances Already Out of Control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.description: For 14 straight years, ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a critical brain region going offline, and moral overconfidence all let good people cross the line step by step.
item.content:encoded:
For 14 straight years, ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a critical brain region going offline, and moral overconfidence all let good people cross the line step by step.

One author is a clinical neuropsychologist, the other has 20 years of experience suing financial advisers; the offender profiles and warning signals here have more screening value than moral slogans.

2:04 The test for crossing the line is one sentence: this is not your money
Moira defines financial misconduct as "doing bad things with other people's money": it includes both taking money for yourself and guiding or advising others to deploy funds in ways that don't serve their best interests. She stresses that anyone working in finance must always remember "this is not your money." Reducing the ethical question to fiduciary duty gives all the later warning signals a single baseline for judgment.

9:10 The number one red flag for 14 straight years is personal financial problems
Philippa cites ACFE's global report: for 14 consecutive years, the top fraud red flag has not been greed but "personal financial problems" — people whose personal finances are out of control, who can't make ends meet, or who are drowning in debt are the most likely to get involved in financial misconduct. The financial industry offers access to other people's money and attracts people who chase wealth, and people are irrational about money on top of that; the three conditions stack into fertile ground for misconduct.

13:14 Listening to advice, the brain acts like it's praying: the critical region goes offline
Moira notes that neuroimaging evidence shows that when people receive financial advice, key critical regions of the brain go "offline," in a state similar to the brain during prayer. People feel safe, trusting, and open, and this non-critical state heightens vulnerability, especially for those unfamiliar with finance. She gives the example that even hedge fund managers will "sit and wait for answers" in front of an adviser rather than pressing on how a product actually works.

19:19 Good people start erring through obedience and helpfulness, not greed
Philippa and Moira break down the path by which good people go wrong: blindly obeying orders, crossing lines out of "misguided helpfulness," then hiding the mistake out of fear, then covering it with a bigger lie. The book's "John" slides from a small slip into lying, then into doubling down on the cover-up. Moira stresses that ethics is not a solo sport but a team sport; if the organizational culture tacitly permits misconduct, it's very hard for an individual to stay clean alone.

37:36 Psychopaths flow into finance disproportionately
Responding to Cameron's concern, Moira says the evidence shows psychopaths flow disproportionately into finance and business because "that's where the money is." She cites Robert Hare's research: successful psychopaths tend to be charming and extremely good at sensing and exploiting other people's desires. The damage they do is large, and they often keep circulating within the industry because colleagues feel a sense of "relief," leaving the problem for the next firm.

53:50 Most people don't realize they're making an ethical decision at all
Traditional ethics training always presents clear moral dilemmas in a classroom, but real-world problems tend to arise quietly, so people don't realize they're at a fork in the road. Moira cites Kahneman's "what you see is all there is": people don't proactively question the motives of product providers, don't think about who benefits from a complex product, and don't admit to themselves that they don't actually understand it. The result is that even with ethics training, most of the time they have no idea they're facing an ethical decision.

1:02:56 The future wrongdoer is a vulnerable ordinary person, not a bad guy
Philippa lists the profile of the future wrongdoer: early in their career (Evan got swept into a global fraud one month into the job and was banned for life nine months later), in debt, highly dependent on their boss, people-pleasing, low self-esteem (compensated for with a luxury car), exhausted, dealing with family problems, and so on. These signals are rarely used by the industry to screen advisers for their own biases; they aren't some rare evil but the shared weaknesses of ordinary people under pressure and vulnerability.

1:09:07 After 20 years of suing, she has never sued a single CFP
Philippa practiced law for 20 years and sued many financial professionals, but never once sued a CFP certificant. She thinks there's no simple way to pick out a good adviser, but holding a certification is a positive signal. She also offers a test: if an adviser only talks about investments and doesn't understand the client's whole life situation, that's just wealth management, not financial planning — the subject of planning is the person, not the assets.

item.title: The 5% Treasury Yield Isn't About Inflation: $32 Trillion of Debt Means Buyers Will Only Take More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.description: Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already full up on Treasuries at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new supply a year, and the Treasury can't hold it down with buybacks either.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already full up on Treasuries at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new supply a year, and the Treasury can't hold it down with buybacks either.

The mainstream narrative pins the 30-year at 5% on inflation; this episode offers a genuinely additive alternative framework and folds the limits of Treasury intervention, the mechanics of Fed balance-sheet runoff, and the term premium debate into one logic.

4:04 5% is first a Treasury interest bill, not a macro signal
Host Joe asks Daryl what he sees when the 30-year Treasury yield is above 5% — even after it ticked down slightly that day following the Fed chair's remarks. Daryl's answer isn't a macro model but the Treasury's predicament: if I were the Treasury secretary, what I'd see is that US government interest expense is extraordinarily high and I have to find a way to push yields down. That line sets the frame for the whole episode: the official side has a strong incentive to push long-end rates down, but whether it can and whether it should are the premises for everything that follows.

5:07 The Treasury wants to sell another $10 billion, it can only pay more
Daryl gives the single most important thought experiment of the segment: suppose there's no inflation risk and no sovereign default, and you're a macro hedge fund that already holds $20 billion of 10-year Treasuries. The Treasury secretary calls and asks you to buy another $10 billion — why won't you? The answer: at a 5.3% yield you've already made the allocation you want, and to get you to add, you have to be paid a higher interest rate as compensation. This logic incidentally explains the structural shift on the demand side — foreign central banks are already full up and no longer buying, so new Treasury supply can only land with domestic free discretionary buyers: banks, pensions, insurers, hedge funds, and that money is highly sensitive to yield.

8:10 The logic didn't change, the debt stock hit a tipping point
Joe raises the objection that has to be faced: aging populations, a political system with no appetite for spending cuts, unsustainable deficits — this bearish logic existed in 2018 and 2019, and Japan was talked about this way for decades before that, so why did yields keep falling then and why are they rising now? Daryl's answer is a scale effect: the 60% debt/GDP red line the IMF drew back then is far behind us, France is already at 100%; the US Treasury market grew from about $18 trillion to $31 trillion and keeps expanding. There's no new logic — the quantity of debt itself has accumulated to a tipping point.

10:13 The main driver of the long end at 5% is issuance, not inflation expectations
Given the short end is still pinned by high inflation and the Fed, why not attribute the high 30-year yield directly to inflation expectations? Daryl concedes inflation over the past five years has indeed been significantly above the Fed's target and the job isn't done, but points out: implied inflation expectations backed out of real versus nominal bonds are not flashing alarm; the investors actually buying and selling 10-, 20- and 30-year Treasuries are not processing inflation first in their heads, but supply relative to demand. He mentions John Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level, but that's a long-run framework — the main driver of the term premium right now is issuance, not prices.

13:18 Buybacks to cap yields are just a signal, and the ammunition is far too small
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an expansion of Treasury buybacks, with the official rationale being liquidity. Daryl reads the subtext directly: from the wording of his public remarks, he doesn't think the problem is market liquidity, he thinks yields are ‘too high’, and he says outright that he's sending a signal to the market. The problem is that the size of Treasury's operations is a drop in the bucket relative to the whole Treasury market, and the market moved briefly on the news then quickly reversed. Trying to hold down the path of yields with the government's own resources has a precedent — the 1992 sterling crisis — and Bessent was the man shorting the pound at Soros's fund back then.

19:22 The real job of buybacks is sweeping up old bonds, not managing rates
The original design of the buyback program was not to manage yields: as the Treasury keeps issuing new securities, a large stock of illiquid off-the-run old bonds is left in the market, clogging dealer balance sheets and trading away from a smooth yield curve. A paper Daryl is working on with two New York Fed economists is testing whether sweeping up the scraps on a ‘regular, predictable’ schedule and swapping in new issues can improve market liquidity and earn taxpayers the gain from buying low and selling high. The phrase ‘odd lots’ happens to be where the show's name comes from. He thinks this routine operation works; the Treasury stepping in at a moment of emergency to defend its own bond market is a different matter.

25:30 The constraint on balance-sheet runoff is reserves, not the asset side
A new Fed chair wants to shrink the balance sheet, but most people only stare at the asset side. Daryl points out the arithmetic constraint: selling assets requires extinguishing an equal amount of liabilities. Of the three liability buckets, the TGA can't have the Treasury pull its deposits out, and currency in circulation can't be recalled, so the only thing that can be squeezed is commercial banks' reserves at the Fed. But today's reserves are the ‘Swiss Army knife of the financial industry’: they pay interest at market rates, satisfy liquidity regulation, and are usable for payments at any time, so banks have no incentive to give them up. The ratchet effect that Acharya and Rajan laid out at Jackson Hole in 2017 already showed this: every time the Fed expands its balance sheet, banks get addicted to reserves, and runoff necessarily causes market volatility.

28:33 The task force will swap duration, not actually shrink the size
Daryl states he has no inside information on the task force, but makes two predictions about the group led by Jeremy Stein: first, the real problem isn't size but composition, and the sensible move is to gradually replace the Fed's long-dated Treasuries with short-dated bills, so that reserve interest expense on the liability side offsets bill interest income on the asset side in the same direction, reducing the hit to the Fed's own P&L from swings in the policy rate; second, don't keep mortgage-backed securities on the asset side — let them roll off naturally. His own conclusion is blunter: the Fed doesn't necessarily have to shrink the balance sheet, but it must have the tools in hand to shrink on its own, or it will be backed into a corner when Congress applies pressure.

item.title: A wallet's profit engine isn't interest on balances, it's money moving inside the system
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.description: The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and money going out can be charged again. It earns the spread on flow, not interest on deposits — PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.
item.content:encoded:
The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and money going out can be charged again. It earns the spread on flow, not interest on deposits — PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.

It takes the wallet cost structure apart for real: wholesale network pricing under ten cents, while platforms can charge users several times that; Japanese players even open accounts at multiple banks to route around clearing. Useful as a business teardown even if you don't do payments.

1:05 A wallet has to answer how it makes money on day one
It opens with the author's own $100 Venmo bill to a barber: for a small transaction that already has a mature payment rail, why does PayPal still want to wedge itself in and monetize it. Then it quickly sets the scope: this is about the e-wallet business, not crypto private-key wallets; a wallet that appears to hold and disburse balances immediately enters the regulatory minefield around deposits, so a wallet has to answer how it makes money from the first day of design — fail that, and the product dies.

5:14 Card fraud isn't scammers building sites, it's leakage at the issuer
The biggest early obstacle to online transactions was that users didn't dare hand over their card numbers, and the media kept amplifying card-fraud risk. The author points out the opposite is true: most fraud comes from massive data breaches at the issuing end, not from scammers parasitizing checkout pages, and concludes that ‘economies of scale protect criminals too’. PayPal's value was standing between the user's card number and the merchant, capping the risk of any single transaction — which gave it grounds to charge a toll near 3%, and planted the seed for the balance design that followed.

6:19 A free wallet is not free at all for the wallet itself
Putting money into a wallet goes through the card networks, at a historical list price of about 3%, and the wallet eats that cost; but once the balance stays inside the system, transfers between users are nearly equivalent to changing one row in a database, too cheap to bill for. PayPal charges close to full price on both the in and out legs, so simply having internal transfers substitute for external ones adds a chunk of gross margin. A wallet that is free to the average user is not free to the wallet — the zero marginal cost of the float is the real dam.

9:21 Driving down network fees makes more money than product innovation
There is no necessary relationship between wholesale and retail: buying millions of ACH transactions costs about $0.05 each, while a payment processor can quote a merchant close to $0.30; the spread is a tax the platform levies on the underlying plumbing. Japan is more extreme: interbank transfers cost about ¥200 per transaction while intra-bank entries are nearly free, so some products open accounts at each of the top banks, let users' money move inside the banks, and settle via daily netting. In finance, driving down network fees converts into wallet profit more directly than product innovation does.

12:27 Cash-out isn't a user perk, it's a second toll pipe
Cash App prices cash-out the same way: want it fast, pick the pricier card rail, charged at 1.75% with a 25-cent minimum; the author tested withdrawing $50 and was quoted 88 cents. Paired with that is issuing prepaid cards through partners like Sutton Bank, so money spent outside the system still captures swipe fees. The wallet no longer treats cash-out as a user benefit but as a second revenue pipe, because the partner bank needs the wallet's user scale and the wallet needs the bank's issuing license.

20:53 On co-brand cards the wallet takes a cut and carries the bad debt
The logic of a wallet co-branding a credit card is charging on both sides, but risk control is the real battlefield: wallets typically assume their accumulated spending data lets them underwrite more accurately than the issuing bank. The industry has repeatedly shown FICO is already strong enough to be hard to displace; the extra variables that could meaningfully improve losses tend to sit on the wrong side of the law. What actually prices the wallet is the agreement — the bank requires the whole loan portfolio's loss rate to stay under a threshold, or the wallet's revenue share goes to zero or even turns negative. The 10-K language dances around ‘loss sharing’, but in essence the wallet is carrying the issuer's bad debt.

24:50 Users care about the phone, not the plastic card
Apple's core argument when negotiating with banks is that users care about the phone, not the plastic credit card; if banks won't pay, Apple can also back or build a new two-sided payment network and take users with it. Reporting puts Apple's take on Apple Pay at 15 basis points per transaction, with Google reportedly taking nothing — the author uses this to gripe about the two giants' differing ability to run non-core products. The next layer is the conclusion that the checkout counter itself can work like ad inventory: once goods and prices are fixed, who gets ranked first among payment methods becomes a bidding war, and Stripe has already replaced the traditional display with dynamic ordering by user preference, even opening up merchant fine-tuning options.

31:13 Network fees don't come down at the table, they come down in the default
Extend Link into a general-ledger-level settlement negotiation layer: if users store their low-cost payment methods in Link, the next checkout can bypass the card networks and go through bank accounts; the network fees saved get redistributed between merchant and user. This can't be negotiated by one company sitting at one table — it's the aggregation of decisions by millions of users and merchants, ultimately representing a bloc on the other side of the payments negotiating table worth close to 1% of global GDP. Only a total that size has the standing to reprice network fees.

item.title: If It Can't Solve Quantum Gravity, It Isn't Real AGI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.description: A physicist draws a high line for AGI: solving quantum gravity is the bar. The conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI — a searched-for material still has to pass the synthesizability gate, and the result may be zero.
item.content:encoded:
A physicist draws a high line for AGI: solving quantum gravity is the bar. The conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI — a searched-for material still has to pass the synthesizability gate, and the result may be zero.

A noise-canceling pass on the AI world's default assumptions: a string theorist makes the returns to science and the boundaries of AI concrete and checkable, useful for calibrating your own time expectations in hard tech. The narrative is a bit slow; the substance is concentrated in the middle and back half.

17:28 Learning too much paralyzes you; only naivety dares ask the original question
The hardest part of going from student to researcher isn't absorbing knowledge, it's posing the original questions that push the boundary of knowledge forward. Gopakumar describes this transition as ‘naivety plus experience’: learning too much paralyzes you, and you need to keep a bit of naivety to dare ask the questions that look impossible to even start. The advisor's job is to teach you to break a big problem into small steps you can advance right now without losing the ultimate goal. His own advisor, David Gross, was good at this — by his account, Gross's first student produced work that won the two of them a Nobel together, and Witten also won a Fields Medal. Now he puts his own students through the same method: he assigns the first one or two problems, problems he himself doesn't have the answer to, and walks with the student slowly through the third and fourth years, then lets them ask their own questions independently.

28:36 Spacetime isn't a background, it's an emergent approximation
Think of string theory the way you think of water being made of discrete atoms: the continuous spacetime we touch is very likely just a low-resolution approximation of some deeper structure at macroscopic scales. Gopakumar stresses this isn't pure speculation — quantum mechanics itself doesn't allow spacetime to be treated as an infinitely divisible smooth background; add black holes (Hawking and others found they have many anomalous properties) and the breakdown of the Big Bang at the singularity, and physicists have to answer ‘where does spacetime come from.’ String theory happens to give a natural framework: spacetime emerges from something more fundamental, and gravity and the known interactions fit inside it too. This explains why he treats ‘solving quantum gravity’ as a very high bar for intelligence: it demands not just doing problems, but building a new conceptual framework.

39:45 Materials should be designed backwards: set the property, then find the structure
Start with a long-horizon yardstick: quantum mechanics was originally just for understanding atoms, and the devices it now underpins account, by his estimate, for roughly 35%-40% of US GDP, while the commercial ripples only became obvious four or five decades after the theory appeared. He calls the current phase the second quantum revolution: quantum materials like graphene, found by accident, are already commercializing, and the next step is inverse materials design with AI — first define what properties a material needs, then search for what structure can deliver them and how to synthesize it, bypassing traditional trial-and-error chemistry. He also shares a conversation with Demis Hassabis: DeepMind's next holy grail is finding a room-temperature superconductor, and Hassabis told him from the start not to talk about quantum gravity.

50:59 Being stuck is the norm; keep three or four problems in the air at once
Being stuck isn't the exception, it's a researcher's daily life; especially in the student-to-researcher transition, being stuck can feel like a crush (being overwhelmed). Gopakumar's first strategy is portfolio hedging: push three or four problems at once, and when one dies, switch to another — probabilistically, one of them will move half a step. The second move is to go teach — the moment a student's eyes light up, that satisfaction can pull you out of a trough, and he has repeatedly found that ‘after a lecture, a stuck problem suddenly opens up.’ The third move is to deliberately learn something new you've always wanted to learn but never had time for, to switch to a new frame of reference before returning to the old problem.

55:08 Talent is multiplicative, not additive; the shortage is never headcount
Why does top science cluster in a few places instead of spreading evenly? Gopakumar gives the mechanism: talking in the same place, using each other as sounding boards, keeps the brain in a stimulated state even without formal collaboration; and once real collaboration happens, the different skills two people bring are multiplicative rather than additive. He borrows a physics metaphor: photons in an ordinary light bulb are chaotic, photons in a laser are coherent with each other, and a group of people that achieves coherence will also produce a lasing effect like a laser. He says many Indian institutions actually underperform their talent, and what's missing isn't headcount but this resonant atmosphere; so ICTS's founding principle is simple — hire only first-rate people, give them resources and freedom, and don't let them lower their ambitions.

1:11:19 AI can accelerate research, but it can't make a conceptual leap
AI just won two Nobel Prizes in a row, but Gopakumar splits ‘AI for science’ and ‘science for AI’ into two things: the former he grants is an overdrive gear, with AI accelerating a very narrow class of tasks in research; but the ‘theory’ AI does today is still far from his conceptual-layer standard, and the best physics relies on conceptual leaps rather than pattern recognition. Conversely, he's more bullish on science for AI — among the people who discovered scaling laws at Anthropic are physicists by training; Hopfield was himself a statistical physicist, using simple physical models to simulate the brain. Along this path, physicists might join computer scientists and neuroscientists to take AI from language models to physics-inspired world models. This distinction is worth remembering.

1:21:32 After the synthesizability gate, zero new AI materials are left
The soberest bucket of cold water in the whole session came from the audience Q&A: Google claims to have discovered a large number of new materials with AI, but after filtering for feasibility and the synthesizability gate, Gopakumar's phrasing is ‘I think left with zero’ — zero left. His stance isn't to deny AI materials science (someone in the same session cited Microsoft's DFT model with only 385,000 parameters that bypasses traditional hybrid methods), but to remind you the whole chain is still long: after predicting a crystal structure you still have to grow it and scale it, and every step can filter out the surprise. He says India should also bet on this chain. That line is a useful reverse calibration for the ‘AI discovers new materials’ narrative.

item.title: AI's Front-Runners Are Just Refineries, Not the Native-App Winners
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.description: AI has entered its agent phase: the first-stage leaders are only refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to conjure something from nothing.
item.content:encoded:
AI has entered its agent phase: the first-stage leaders are only refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to conjure something from nothing.

Zeng Ming uses a three-stage industrial history to give you a coordinate system for judging where AI stands — an antidote to the optimism of "this time is different" — and lays out both the opportunity window for application founders and the brutal expectations for incumbents' transformation.

16:28 Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of a general-purpose technology into three stages: first it becomes social infrastructure, then applications explode, and finally native applications appear. In 2026, token becoming a consensus unit of measurement shows the first stage has matured; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called "lobster") mark AI's formal entry into the agent stage. He draws an analogy to the 1992 website-building movement: people then were building websites to share information, today they are building agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet, and whoever can establish agent standards and seize the user entry point may be the biggest opportunity of the next two years.

27:49 A ten-trillion-dollar company will appear, but not these two
Zeng Ming says plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technological and commercial achievements, but business history shows the first wave of breakout companies is most likely not the big winners of the native-application stage. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, AOL was valued at $220 billion, and neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that refine crude oil — the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies, and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly exist in the future, but it may not be the two currently leading. Model companies will move toward a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

1:10:29 The unit of an AI-native organization is the task, not the job
The company corresponds to the industrial-age hierarchy; AI overturns the industrial age, and the corporate system will wither. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not the job but the task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around "what needs to be solved," with humans and AI collaborating around tasks. So well-designed jobs and levels will disappear, and the traditional middle layer will die too; future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form, and OpenAI itself is more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of the new organization is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, no longer relying on commands and performance reviews.

1:31:32 Excellence can only be judged in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
Zeng Ming argues that "good ≠ great." Being good is growth that keeps getting positive feedback, while greatness requires overcoming negative feedback again and again, persisting when everyone disapproves, and finally proving through enormous success that you were the era's prophet — so "greatness is judged in hindsight." Good people easily fall into a loop of proving themselves, which makes their strategies conservative. Great people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the times and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders he asks, "Ten years from now, what kind of self would you be satisfied with?" If the answer is "a ten-billion-dollar company," that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly great founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

1:47:24 Strategy in the AI era can't be planned, only generated
Strategy in the AI era is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": the organization must build an environment and network in which strategic insight emerges naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are higher, a CEO cannot plan by linear extrapolation, nor can strategy be outsourced to McKinsey — McKinsey's explosion was a product of the slow maturation of the industrial age. His methodology is "look ten years out, think three years out, act one year out," with the core being "think three years out": you must at least see two or three milestones, creating tension between short-term action and the mid-term picture. Organization-building must ensure enough context rather than control, letting the right people make the right decisions at the right time.

2:01:39 The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
Zeng Ming believes robots are still in a strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. The current two paths — build a generalized brain first or close the scenario loop first — are both logically valid, and it's impossible to judge in advance which is faster. By historical analogy, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and only entered scale when Ford built the assembly line in 1913; robots haven't yet reached their Model T moment, and whoever actually sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented came countless categories like refrigerators, washing machines, and air conditioners, and robots interacting in the physical world will have N kinds of big scenarios — home, companionship, and industry could each produce their own native giant.

2:03:39 The incumbents who feel safe are the least safe
Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave no one is safe, and feeling safe is the most unsafe thing of all. In business history, no era's companies have ever transitioned smoothly into the next era; IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that overturns the industrial revolution, not a continuity innovation like mobile internet, so old giants' technology reserves and organizational culture are negative assets. Google can live on as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is likewise not naturally safe. The new platform will most likely be created by a new company.

2:20:56 Human value lies in conjuring something from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI, and people are on one hand forced and on the other finally liberated to develop new potential. That potential is called creativity — not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and conjure something from nothing. AI has already taken away all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. So he calls his own mission "to be a happy researcher," and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity, forcing even the education system to shift from "knowledge indoctrination" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

item.title: AI writing's moat isn't the model, it's the proprietary data you feed it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/

item.description: Over two years, the writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during a layoff into a one-person content company and a compounding editor; the core method isn't prompts, it's using proprietary experience to cover the "last mile" the model can't reach.
item.content:encoded:
Over two years, the writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during a layoff into a one-person content company and a compounding editor; the core method isn't prompts, it's using proprietary experience to cover the "last mile" the model can't reach.

Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer uses AI as a mode of production: the substance is concentrated in the last 30 minutes, and the personal story up front provides the motivational context.

2:09 The biggest value of an AI coach isn't saving money
After being laid off she was at a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20-a-month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing out her thoughts and letting AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalise her thinking, fight catastrophising, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of that experience wasn't the money saved, but that it made her believe AI really can drive concrete change in a life. At the time she was wavering over whether to take Every's freelance offer, and it was ChatGPT that gave her the push to just try it.

8:26 Throughput comes from upfront context, not clever prompts
She once took on a delivery load of 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She could do it not because she knew a cleverer one-sentence prompt, but because she did a lot of upfront context engineering: feeding the model brand information, product details, audience profiles and differentiators all at once. Much of the demand was essentially content repurposing, and AI is good at rewriting one long piece into versions for different platforms. The rule she distilled: set the scene well up front, and only then can you move fast later.

11:28 Give the model a fence first, then talk tone and word choice
Before Claude Projects existed, she could only keep persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into context each time. This structure didn't fall from the sky; it comes from the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what the pain points are, how the product maps to them, who the competitors are and where the differentiators lie. She says this amounts to giving the model a playground with a fence: first make sure it won't wander off, then talk about word choice, tone and reading difficulty. Later, as soon as Projects launched, she built a separate project for every client and every column.

15:40 AI writing's last mile can only be covered by a human
She believes there is a "last mile" problem in AI writing: models have a knowledge cutoff, and they aren't in the real physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just throw the model a single line like "write a blog post about style guides", all you'll get is the generic content it already knows, which is commoditised information; what really makes writing unique is fresh ingredients the model has never seen, like internal company research, third-party reports and personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; the human is responsible for supplying good ingredients.

22:50 AI's value is reducing friction, not speeding up output
She talks openly about her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't just producing content faster, but reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care doctor for three years, and eventually just had Codex find doctors who accept her insurance and are taking new patients and complete the booking; email is first filtered by automation, and only messages that genuinely need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't treating AI as a production tool, but as assistive technology that makes her day-to-day running "as a person" easier.

27:03 Let AI interview you repeatedly, and it can prioritise for you
Two years ago she just asked ChatGPT whether it could be her career coach; today that coach lives in a Codex project containing her role profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a folder of reader praise and her OKRs. She doesn't maintain the board herself; she uses voice conversation to have the system prioritise by highest impact, and the system also maintains her Kanban for her. The key to building this system is letting AI interview her repeatedly, then sedimenting the interview content into context. She says it's like having a Chief of Staff, not just a writer.

32:27 Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted
The core of the Compound Writing plugin is compounding thinking: every piece of feedback given to AI should flow back into the system so the next output is automatically better. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and adapted it into a writing workflow: code and writing both have brainstorming, planning, drafting and review stages, except writing focuses more on structure, voice and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit that looks at big structure and argument, a line edit that works sentence by sentence, and a final pass that checks before publication. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window, but pours the day's fresh material into this system.

39:19 Vonnegut as editor gives you a perspective, not a verdict
She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's principle of suspense about the bomb under the table, and the expressive styles of Sorkin and Sedaris into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks whether "the story starts as close to the end as possible" and whether "every sentence earns its place"; Hitchcock's perspective asks whether the reader will want to keep reading because of this. She stresses that this isn't letting the masters' ghosts mark up your draft, but giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject; non-professional writers may actually benefit more, because they're less likely to be picking at themselves while they write.

item.title: Stronger Models Make Dirty Data Deadlier: Cleaning Is Worth More, Not Less
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.description: Jane Street's alternative data team found that once data leaks future information into the past, the stronger the model, the more dangerous it gets; pinning down "what was known at the time" is worth more than tuning the model.
item.content:encoded:
Jane Street's alternative data team found that once data leaks future information into the past, the stronger the model, the more dangerous it gets; pinning down "what was known at the time" is worth more than tuning the model.

This episode is a dense account of how data engineering actually creates value; the second half, on corrected data, timestamps and cost models, contains judgments you won't hear in most AI discussions.

2:06 Once a pattern is found, competition eats it
This is what Eric defines as an anti-inductive environment: in trading, the patterns you find are often quickly absorbed by other people and the market, and then stop working; knowledge that can accumulate over the long term like a law of physics is rare. Because of this, the signal-to-noise ratio of trading data is inherently ugly — the whole mechanism of the market is to keep squeezing out extractable signal, and what's left drifts closer and closer to a random walk. To keep winning, you have to keep finding new facts, not sit on old patterns.

19:21 Prices can go negative, so don't hard-code assumptions into the system
On April 20, 2020, the settlement price of near-expiry crude oil futures on the CME closed negative — just for that one day, and the final settlement price later returned to positive. The reason wasn't that oil had no value, but that storage space at the delivery point, Cushing, was nearly full and nobody wanted to take physical delivery. Order and risk systems that had long assumed prices must be positive failed on the spot: some people couldn't place orders, others didn't know how to handle negative returns. Eric's conclusion is that a large part of trading is understanding the boring details of reality: tank capacity, contract multipliers, quote units. Only when the system gets these details right can you draw a ceiling on risk.

32:33 Domain experts don't know how good good tools can be
For data and systems to be genuinely usable, the bottleneck is often not writing code but translation. Eric observes that traders have a high tolerance for painful workflows, worn down by Excel and manual processes to the point where they don't know they deserve better tools; conversely, software engineers who don't understand the trading domain can only build to a narrow spec. So his job is to explain the domain's real mechanics to engineers, and to explain "how good it could get" to traders. Jane Street now has such an embedded developer on every desk, and that role grew out of exactly this.

59:04 The number of parking spaces is not the sales figure
The classic example of alternative data is counting cars in Walmart parking lots — the fuller the cars, the better the business. Eric says this example is actually terrible: what you want to infer is spending, and parking spaces only tell you foot traffic, very indirectly; about 20% of Walmart's shopping happens online, and a city like New York has no parking lots to count. The more direct signal is on the transaction side: card-issuing banks, the Visa/Mastercard networks, and credit union processing systems know how much people actually spent, and can sell anonymised aggregate statistics to buyers.

1:04:08 Corrected data turns a backtest into a time machine
When deciding "should we subscribe to this dataset," the vendor may already have corrected past errors; backtesting on the pretty corrected data doesn't test the data you would actually have received back then, but the right answers you only learned later. Eric says this is equivalent to simulating that you have a time machine. Jane Street's solution is to keep every piece of raw data and the local timestamp at which it arrived, so that no matter how many transformations you do later, you can reconstruct "what exactly we knew at that moment." This is the same logic as distrusting exchange timestamps and trusting only your own data's arrival time.

1:08:10 LLMs know the future, so keep them off historical data
AI hits alternative data on two levels: stronger predictive models raise the value of good data, and LLMs make it easy to extract features from text. But watch out for a causal trap — using the latest LLM to featurize old documents drags in what happened later: it knows how Enron ended, and it may have seen later revisions of this financial report in its training data. This creates a new future-information leak, and when handling historical data you especially need to pin down "which point-in-time model was used."

1:11:26 The stronger the model, the more data cleaning is worth
A common expectation is that as neural networks get stronger, feature engineering and manual cleaning will be replaced. Eric's view is the opposite: once models can do more on their own, you can do less manual feature work, but the data you feed in has to be more correct. If the data isn't point-in-time and quietly leaks future information into the past, stronger models will learn that problem; different models also have different tolerances for outliers and patches of dirty data. All told, cleaning data is worth more, not less.

1:16:34 Usage-based billing pushes teams to keep saving money
Jane Street runs its data warehouse in its own data centre, and it isn't purely about control. Eric's observation: move the same queries to a cloud vendor billed by reads or compute time, and the price is high enough that you'd think "this money could buy a pile of hardware." More important is the distorting effect of the cost model — usage-based billing makes teams constantly optimise the bill and reshape workloads to accommodate the billing; once self-hosted, cost becomes a one-off hardware investment, and the team spends its time on research and queries themselves rather than on saving money.
