item.description: The Fed's credibility broke over a single meeting with no hike, while the options market still prices Fed day like any other day — the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.
item.content:encoded:
The Fed's credibility broke over a single meeting with no hike, while the options market still prices Fed day like any other day — the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.

Three pieces of evidence — sticky inflation, the midterms, and Fed credibility — point at the same thing: volatility is too low and cheap protection is a mirage. The frameworks and the data are both concrete.

3:03 A Fed without forward guidance is flipping a coin
Both hosts open with the change: at past FOMC meetings the market knew the odds well in advance, but this time the probability of a hike at the next meeting is only 55 to 45 — barely better than a coin flip. Add Warsh's Jackson Hole statement that he wants to fade forward guidance, and every meeting from here can turn into ‘wait for the outcome, then react.’ Rate surprises transmit through debt and leverage into every asset, so volatility has to be repriced. The hosts also assert, based on history, that once the market truly tests them, nearly every official eventually folds — so this current commitment to ‘never give the market expectations in advance’ is itself the variable most worth testing.

17:31 Midterm volatility is priced as just another day
Kevin Muir thinks midterm volatility is badly underpriced. During the 2022 midterms, the options market priced a single-day S&P move of ±1.8% for voting day; in 2018 it was ±1.25%; now it is only ±0.9%. And this time Trump's approval is at historic lows, and he just spent an hour in a primetime address talking about ‘election fraud,’ as if paving the way to challenge the result. Muir is careful to say: it's fine if you think he's overthinking it — as voting day approaches, the question of whether the election gets roiled will itself be repriced. With volatility near seasonal lows and implied correlation also at historic lows, the odds on being long volatility are far better than usual.

23:41 The inflation pullback is a supply illusion; demand hasn't cooled
Ahan Manon breaks the PCE components into ‘demand-driven’ and ‘supply-driven.’ Right now the contributions are 3.31 versus 0.38; even if you strip out the energy supply shock from the Iran situation entirely, the remaining demand side alone is enough to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target. Historically, demand-driven inflation is slow and persistent, while supply-driven inflation tends to spike fast and mean-revert within 6 to 12 months. The bigger problem is breadth: in recent months, 70% to 80% of PCE components rose more than 2%. June briefly went negative month-over-month and July only rebounded 16 basis points, but that short-term cooling came almost entirely from the supply side; the demand-driven trend has not been interrupted.

34:51 The credibility one hike would have fixed, he didn't do
Ben Hunt says Warsh threw an ‘own goal’ at the press conference after the July meeting. The new face and the hawkish inflation talk had repaired the ‘Fed credibility’ narrative substantially; but what was actually needed was an immediate 25 basis point hike. Do that one time and the market believes ‘he means what he says,’ and you never need to hike repeatedly afterward. Skip that step and the narrative flips completely: every independent piece that appeared in the financial media that week was saying the same thing in different words — ‘meet the new boss, same as the old boss.’ Once credibility shatters it is hard to glue back; the August gold rally was precisely the market's reaction to ‘hawkish talk, no action.’

40:13 After credibility is damaged, only verbal financial repression is left
Ben Hunt lists four pressures the Fed and Treasury must handle but absolutely cannot let blow up: the Iran war has no easy exit and oil stays higher for longer; fiscal stimulus effects fade and tariff pressure returns; the insurance sector has a systemic problem of captive insurers being used to warehouse private investments; and 10-year and 30-year long-end yields above all cannot be pushed higher by the market. Any one of them could be the fuse for the next financial crisis. Handling them requires credibility, and credibility has just been damaged, so every policy option left is ‘verbal financial repression’ — using statements and intervention to hold yields down rather than letting the market price them. His judgment: this operation has no maturity date, it only accelerates.

49:25 The options market treats a Fed meeting as an ordinary day
The options term structure Brent Kachuba shows has almost no event risk: the S&P 0DTE straddle on the day of Warsh's speech was worth only 38 index points; SPX options expiring August 31 carried implied volatility of just 7%, the overall term structure sat at a 90-day low, and put open interest was very low. He normally avoids trading Fed events, because an event turns options into a kind of ‘tax’ — you collect premium before the event, and the moment it passes time value decays. But the special thing this time is that the market has crushed expected volatility to near zero and nobody is buying protection; before Jackson Hole he bought a few ‘lottery tickets’ with very cheap short-dated put spreads, because if Warsh says one thing the market doesn't want to hear, naked option sellers get flattened instantly. Once the event passes is the better time to chase directional trends.

58:42 Outsource the writing and you outsource the thinking
The closing topic is the Druckenmiller column handed to the WSJ: he said publicly it was written with AI, for the simple reason that AI writes better than he does. The two hosts argue the core question is whether the views and the emotion belong to the author; Druckenmiller's piece reads like his usual intuitive judgment, with AI only organizing and expressing it, so it isn't deception. Ben Hunt draws the line at the writing itself: writing is part of the thinking process, ‘I write it down to figure out what I think.’ When the text-generation step is outsourced, readers lose an important clue — whether the author has actually thought these words through. Investment blogs are already full of obvious AI output; judging whether an opinion is reliable can't rest on whether the prose is pretty, but on whether the view has a thinking process behind it.

item.title: China's Economic Peak Is Behind It: Credit Stalls, Deflation Looms

item.content:encoded:
China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has fallen since; credit growth has dropped from 18% to 5%, real growth may be just 1.5%-2%, and the US has outperformed for five straight years. The supply-chain-dominance narrative is falsified by the data, and the future looks more like Japanese-style deflation.

It rebuts the mainstream narrative that China's new industries are a growth engine, grounding the judgment in verifiable credit, special-bond and demographic data; suited to anyone updating their long-term view of the US and China.

0:05 China has already missed its window to overtake the US
Dmitri sets the frame with official data: China's share of global GDP peaked at 18.5% in 2021 and has declined every year since; the US rose from 24% to about 26%. From this he concludes that not only is it nearly impossible for China to replace the US as the world's largest economy, but America's economic advantage may keep widening over the next decade. Logan agrees completely and steers the discussion toward a framework of decay rather than collapse.

2:11 The root of China's slowdown is that credit expansion is over
Logan attributes China's slowdown to the end of extraordinary credit expansion. In the eight years after the financial crisis, China added credit equal to one-third of global GDP; credit growth fell from an average of 18% in 2007-2016 to 9% after 2017, and is now slightly above 5%. Once credit stops, borrowers cannot refinance and investment decelerates. Officials still report 5.2% growth for 2023 and 5% for 2024 and 2025, but he estimates real growth since 2022 at only 1.5%-2%, already below the US.

6:14 Measuring by purchasing power parity amounts to rewarding deflation
To the common rebuttal that China has already surpassed the US on purchasing power parity, Logan says PPP comparisons still make sense for developing countries but do not hold between the world's two largest economies: scoring by PPP amounts to rewarding China for manufacturing deflation — the lower domestic prices are, the stronger the economy looks, when deflation is precisely the problem. He also stresses that debt is repaid in nominal local currency, so nominal GDP is what matters; and the exchange rate is not an exogenous variable but an external signal of China's policy capacity.

13:25 Capital controls are not a cure, they only buy time
Logan concedes that China's capital controls do work, but argues they are no panacea for a giant macroeconomic imbalance. The impossible trinity dictates that free capital movement, exchange-rate stability and independent monetary policy can be achieved at most two at a time. The function of capital controls is to slow outflows, suppress rapid cross-border volatility, and channel outflows into channels the government can see — Huawei and BYD can go abroad in a big way, while the overseas M&A of private firms like HNA in 2016 was halted. These are two sides of the same screening mechanism.

17:35 Credit is still subsidising old industries, not shifting to new ones
Logan rebuts the claim that credit is shifting toward higher-productivity new industries: central bank data show the share of loans issued at or below the Loan Prime Rate has risen from the low 20s percent to 59%, meaning banks are continuously subsidising. The share of special revenue bonds going to so-called strategic industries rose only from about 2% in 2021 to 6% in 2025, with the vast majority still flowing to traditional sectors. Using the 2023 input-output tables, EVs, batteries, AI and solar together come to roughly 6.3% of GDP, while the decline in property and infrastructure investment is about six times the increment from these new industries.

27:45 Europe is the last buyer of China's excess capacity
Logan judges that if Europe turns protectionist, China is "really finished": the US market has already narrowed and there is limited room for transshipment, and the developing world cannot absorb China's excess capacity while sustaining its own growth. He warns that the US is wrong to focus only on the bilateral deficit — the deficit is determined by the savings-investment gap, and tariffs merely redistribute it; failing to address the underlying imbalance will only spawn more transshipment trade.

34:58 Without tax reform, domestic demand cannot get up off the floor
Logan draws a parallel with the Kosygin reforms in the Soviet Union: Brezhnev chose a turn toward the scientific-technological revolution over pushing reform and preserving ideology. For China to convert savings into consumption, the real lever is tax policy — extracting resources from high-net-worth individuals, state-owned enterprises and private firms shut out of the financial system. But he thinks it is nearly unimaginable that Xi Jinping would go on television and declare that the fiscal and financial system of the past 15 years no longer applies; Beijing sticks to the 5% growth narrative partly to undermine export controls and to deter Western investment in alternative supply chains.

39:00 China in 2035 will look like Japan today
Logan predicts that absent a dramatic policy shift, China's economy in 2035 will look more like Japan's: persistent deflation, persistent external surpluses, downward pressure on the exchange rate and low interest rates. The hardest constraint is demography — China's actual average age at death is 73, and the baby boom at the founding of the PRC will bring a decline of 50-60 million people over the next decade, about 3%-4% of the total population; even holding the birth rate at last year's low of 7.92 million will not stop it. He also notes the fiscal deficit is already close to $2 trillion a year, 9.5% of GDP, leaving far fewer resources to draw on than in the past. Finally, he says that if China really did win on export share, it would only provoke a stronger political backlash — "winning is losing."
